knowledge.text: Python is a programming language.
A computer is an electronic machine that processes information.
Programming is the process of writing instructions for computers.
Machine learning is a method where software learns patterns from data.
Data is information that can be stored and processed.
A file is a collection of information stored on a computer.
A program is a set of instructions executed by a computer.
An algorithm is a sequence of steps used to solve a problem.
A variable is a named place used to store a value in a program.
A function is a reusable block of program instructions.
PYTHON KNOWLEDGE BASE
SUBJECT is Python Programming
PURPOSE is Structured knowledge for an autonomous text-learning system
SECTION 1: PYTHON OVERVIEW
Python is a high-level general-purpose programming language.
Python is widely used for automation, web development, data analysis, scientific computing, scripting, education, testing, and artificial intelligence.
Python was created by Guido van Rossum.
Python emphasizes readability and relatively simple syntax.
Python programs are commonly stored in files ending with .py.
Python source code is normally executed by a Python interpreter.
Python is dynamically typed.
Python uses strong type rules even though variable types do not normally need to be declared.
Python supports procedural programming.
Python supports object-oriented programming.
Python supports functional programming techniques.
Python includes a large standard library.
Python packages can extend the standard library.
Python uses indentation to define blocks of code.
Python comments begin with the hash character.
A Python statement usually represents an operation performed by the program.
A Python expression produces a value.
A Python variable is a name associated with an object.
Python objects have identity, type, and value.
Everything represented as a value in Python is an object.
Programming is the process of giving a computer precise instructions.
A programming language provides rules for expressing instructions and data.
Syntax describes how valid Python code must be written.
Semantics describes what valid Python code means or does.
An interpreter executes Python code.
Readability is important because programs are maintained and modified by humans.
Python uses indentation to represent code blocks.
Python variables refer to objects.
Python expressions produce values.
Python statements perform actions or control execution.
Python has dynamic typing.
Python has strong typing.
Python supports multiple programming paradigms.
SECTION 2: BASIC SYNTAX
Python statements can be written one per line.
Python normally does not require semicolons at the end of statements.
Python uses indentation instead of braces to define blocks.
Consistent indentation is required.
Four spaces are the conventional indentation amount.
A colon commonly introduces an indented block.
Function definitions use the def keyword.
Class definitions use the class keyword.
Conditional blocks use if, elif, and else.
Loop blocks use for and while.
Exception handling blocks use try, except, else, and finally.
Context managers commonly use the with keyword.
A simple Python statement is print("Hello").
A variable assignment is name = "Alice".
A conditional begins with if condition:.
A function begins with def function_name():.
Code belonging to a block must be indented consistently.
A colon after a block header indicates that an indented block follows.
Python identifiers should normally use descriptive names.
A Python single-line comment begins with #.
Comments are ignored by the Python interpreter.
Comments can explain why code exists.
Comments can document assumptions and unusual behavior.
Excessive comments can make code harder to read if they merely repeat obvious code.
Python does not have a dedicated multiline comment syntax.
Triple-quoted strings can be used as multiline strings.
Triple-quoted strings can serve as documentation strings when placed appropriately.
# This is a Python comment.
"""This is a triple-quoted string."""
A docstring is documentation stored in a string associated with a module, class, or function.
Comments explain code to humans.
Docstrings provide structured documentation for Python objects.
A variable name can refer to an object.
Assignment binds a name to a value.
Python variables do not require explicit type declarations in ordinary code.
A variable can be rebound to an object of another type.
Variable names are case-sensitive.
Python identifiers can contain letters, digits, and underscores.
An identifier cannot normally begin with a digit.
Python keywords cannot be used as ordinary variable names.
Descriptive variable names improve readability.
age = 15
name = "Milo"
score = 95
active = True
age can refer to an integer object.
name can refer to a string object.
score can refer to a numeric object.
active can refer to a Boolean object.
Use snake_case for ordinary Python variable and function names.
Avoid single-letter variable names except in small, obvious contexts.
Avoid naming variables after built-in functions such as list, str, id, or sum.
SECTION 5: PYTHON DATA TYPES
Python has built-in numeric types including int, float, and complex.
Python has the Boolean type bool.
Python has the string type str.
Python has the bytes type.
Python has the NoneType type with the value None.
Python has sequence types including list, tuple, range, str, bytes, and bytearray.
Python has mapping types including dict.
Python has set types including set and frozenset.
A data type determines the kind of value an object represents and the operations supported by that object.
Type checking can be performed with type().
isinstance() can test whether an object is an instance of a specified type or class.
type(5) returns int.
type(3.14) returns float.
type("hello") returns str.
type(True) returns bool.
type(None) returns NoneType.
int represents integers.
Python integers can represent arbitrarily large integers subject to available memory.
Integer literals can be positive, negative, or zero.
Python supports decimal integer literals.
Python supports binary integer literals using the 0b prefix.
Python supports octal integer literals using the 0o prefix.
Python supports hexadecimal integer literals using the 0x prefix.
10 is an integer.
0b1010 represents the integer 10.
0xFF represents the integer 255.
SECTION 7: FLOATING-POINT NUMBERS
float represents floating-point numbers.
Floating-point arithmetic can contain small precision errors.
A decimal literal containing a decimal point normally creates a float.
Scientific notation can represent floating-point values.
math.isclose() can be useful when comparing floating-point values.
3.14 is a float.
1.0 is a float.
1e3 represents 1000.0.
Do not assume every decimal floating-point calculation is exactly represented in binary.
Use an appropriate tolerance when comparing calculated floating-point values.
SECTION 8: BOOLEAN VALUES
Python has two Boolean values: True and False.
bool is a subclass of int.
Boolean expressions commonly result from comparisons.
and performs logical conjunction.
or performs logical disjunction.
not negates a Boolean value.
5 > 3 evaluates to True.
5 == 3 evaluates to False.
True and False evaluates to False.
True or False evaluates to True.
not True evaluates to False.
True represents a true Boolean condition.
False represents a false Boolean condition.
None is a special Python singleton representing the absence of a value.
A function that reaches the end without returning a value returns None.
None is commonly used to represent missing, unknown, or intentionally absent data.
None should normally be compared using is or is not.
result = None
if result is None: print("No result")
Prefer value is None over value == None.
SECTION 10: STRINGS
str represents text.
Python strings are sequences of Unicode characters.
Python strings are immutable.
Strings can be enclosed in single quotes.
Strings can be enclosed in double quotes.
Triple quotes can represent multiline strings.
Strings support indexing.
Strings support slicing.
Strings support iteration.
Strings support many useful methods.
f-strings provide formatted string literals.
"hello" is a string.
'hello' is a string.
"""hello""" is a multiline string.
f"Score: {score}" is an f-string.
Strings are sequences.
Strings are immutable.
String indexing returns characters.
String slicing returns substrings.
SECTION 11: STRING OPERATIONS
len(string) returns the number of characters.
string.lower() returns a lowercase version.
string.upper() returns an uppercase version.
string.strip() removes surrounding whitespace.
string.split() splits a string into a list.
separator.join(items) combines strings.
string.replace(old, new) replaces occurrences.
string.startswith(prefix) checks a prefix.
string.endswith(suffix) checks a suffix.
string.find(value) searches for a substring.
string.count(value) counts occurrences.
string.isdigit() tests whether characters are digits.
string.isalpha() tests whether characters are alphabetic.
string.isalnum() tests whether characters are alphanumeric.
"HELLO".lower() produces "hello".
"hello".upper() produces "HELLO".
" hello ".strip() produces "hello".
"a,b,c".split(",") produces ["a", "b", "c"].
"-".join(["a", "b", "c"]) produces "a-b-c".
SECTION 12: STRING FORMATTING
f-strings are commonly used for readable string formatting.
Expressions can appear inside curly braces in f-strings.
Format specifications can control width, precision, alignment, and representation.
str.format() provides another formatting mechanism.
Percent formatting is an older formatting mechanism.
f"Hello {name}"
f"Score: {score:.2f}"
Prefer f-strings for most modern Python string formatting.
SECTION 13: LISTS
list represents an ordered mutable collection.
Lists can contain objects of different types.
Lists support indexing.
Lists support slicing.
Lists can be changed after creation.
Lists can contain duplicate values.
Lists preserve insertion order.
Lists can be nested.
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]
mixed = [1, "hello", True, None]
A list is mutable.
A list is ordered.
A list can contain duplicate values.
A list supports indexing.
A list supports slicing.
SECTION 14: LIST METHODS
append(value) adds one item to the end of a list.
extend(iterable) adds multiple items.
insert(index, value) inserts an item.
remove(value) removes the first matching value.
pop() removes and returns the last item by default.
pop(index) removes and returns an item at an index.
clear() removes all items.
index(value) finds the first matching index.
count(value) counts occurrences.
sort() sorts a list in place.
reverse() reverses a list in place.
copy() creates a shallow copy of a list.
list.sort() changes the existing list.
sorted(list) creates and returns a new sorted list.
SECTION 15: TUPLES
tuple represents an ordered immutable collection.
Tuples support indexing.
Tuples support slicing.
Tuples can contain duplicate values.
Tuples can contain mutable objects even though the tuple itself is immutable.
Tuples can be unpacked into variables.
A one-item tuple requires a trailing comma.
single = (5,)
A tuple is immutable.
A tuple is similar to a list but cannot have its elements reassigned or removed directly.
SECTION 16: SETS
set represents a collection of unique hashable objects.
Sets do not provide indexing by position.
Sets are useful for membership testing.
Sets support union.
Sets support intersection.
Sets support difference.
Sets support symmetric difference.
Sets automatically eliminate duplicate values.
set([1, 1, 2, 2, 3]) produces a set containing 1, 2, and 3.
Sets contain unique elements.
Sets are useful for removing duplicates.
Sets are useful for fast membership testing.
SECTION 17: DICTIONARIES
dict represents a mapping of keys to values.
Dictionary keys must be hashable.
Dictionary values can be any normal Python object.
Dictionaries preserve insertion order.
Dictionaries can be modified.
Dictionaries can store nested dictionaries.
Dictionaries can store lists as values.
Dictionaries provide efficient key-based lookup.
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 15}
person["name"] accesses the value associated with "name".
dict.get(key) retrieves a value and can provide a default.
dict.keys() provides dictionary keys.
dict.values() provides dictionary values.
dict.items() provides key-value pairs.
dict.update() updates entries.
dict.pop() removes an entry.
dict.setdefault() retrieves or creates an entry.
A dictionary maps keys to values.
Dictionary lookup is based on keys rather than numeric positions.
SECTION 18: INDEXING
Python sequences use zero-based indexing.
The first item normally has index 0.
Negative indexes count from the end.
Index -1 refers to the last item.
Index -2 refers to the second-to-last item.
["a", "b", "c"][0] produces "a".
["a", "b", "c"][-1] produces "c".
SECTION 19: SLICING
Sequence slicing uses start:stop:step syntax.
The stop position is normally excluded.
Omitting start begins from the beginning.
Omitting stop continues to the end.
A negative step can reverse traversal.
numbers[1:4] selects positions 1 through 3.
numbers[:3] selects the first three elements.
numbers[3:] selects from position 3 onward.
numbers[::2] selects every second element.
text[::-1] can reverse a string.
SECTION 20: MUTABILITY
Mutable objects can be changed after creation.
Immutable objects cannot be changed after creation.
Lists are mutable.
Dictionaries are mutable.
Sets are mutable.
Tuples are immutable.
Integers are immutable.
Floats are immutable.
Boolean values are immutable.
list is mutable.
dict is mutable.
set is mutable.
str is immutable.
tuple is immutable.
int is immutable.
float is immutable.
SECTION 21: OPERATORS
+ performs addition or sequence concatenation depending on operands.
performs subtraction.
* performs multiplication or repetition depending on operands.
/ performs true division.
// performs floor division.
% calculates the remainder.
** performs exponentiation.
== compares values.
!= tests inequality.
< tests whether the left value is smaller.
> tests whether the left value is larger.
<= tests less-than-or-equal.
>= tests greater-than-or-equal.
= performs assignment.
+= performs augmented addition assignment.
= performs augmented subtraction assignment.
*= performs augmented multiplication assignment.
/= performs augmented division assignment.
10 / 4 produces 2.5.
10 // 4 produces 2.
2 ** 3 produces 8.
SECTION 22: IDENTITY AND MEMBERSHIP
is tests object identity.
is not tests that two references do not refer to the same object.
in tests membership.
not in tests non-membership.
== tests value equality.
is does not generally mean value equality.
"a" in "cat" evaluates to True.
3 in [1, 2, 3] evaluates to True.
Use == for value comparison.
Use is when identity matters, especially for None.
SECTION 23: CONDITIONALS
if executes a block when a condition is true.
elif checks additional conditions.
else executes when preceding conditions are false.
Conditions can use comparison operators.
Conditions can use Boolean operators.
Conditional expressions can select between two values.
if controls conditional execution.
elif provides additional conditional branches.
else provides a fallback branch.
SECTION 24: TRUTHINESS
Python uses truth-value testing in conditions.
False is falsey.
None is falsey.
Numeric zero is falsey.
Empty strings are falsey.
Empty lists are falsey.
Empty tuples are falsey.
Empty dictionaries are falsey.
Empty sets are falsey.
Most non-empty objects are truthy.
if items: checks whether items is truthy.
if not items: checks whether items is falsey.
SECTION 25: FOR LOOPS
A for loop iterates over an iterable.
Lists are iterable.
Strings are iterable.
Tuples are iterable.
Dictionaries are iterable.
Sets are iterable.
range objects are iterable.
for loops can unpack tuples.
for loops can use enumerate().
for loops can use zip().
for index, name in enumerate(names)
print(index, name)
for a, b in zip(list_a, list_b)
SECTION 26: WHILE LOOPS
A while loop repeats while its condition remains true.
A while loop should normally have a way to eventually terminate.
Infinite loops can occur when a loop condition never becomes false.
Check loop conditions carefully to avoid unintended infinite loops.
SECTION 27: BREAK CONTINUE PASS
break exits the nearest enclosing loop.
continue skips to the next loop iteration.
pass performs no operation and can act as a placeholder.
break changes loop control by terminating the loop.
continue changes loop control by skipping the remaining body.
pass does not terminate or repeat a loop.
SECTION 28: RANGE
range() produces a range object.
range can specify stop.
range can specify start and stop.
range can specify start, stop, and step.
The stop value is excluded.
range is commonly used for numeric iteration.
range(5) represents 0 through 4.
range(2, 6) represents 2 through 5.
range(0, 10, 2) represents 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8.
SECTION 29: FUNCTIONS
A function is a reusable block of code.
Functions are defined using def.
Functions can accept parameters.
Functions can return values.
return ends the current function execution.
A function without an explicit return returns None.
Functions create local scopes.
Function parameters receive arguments when the function is called.
Parameters belong to a function definition.
Arguments are values supplied when calling a function.
return sends a value from a function to its caller.
SECTION 30: FUNCTION PARAMETERS
Positional arguments are matched by position.
Keyword arguments are matched by parameter name.
Functions can have default parameter values.
*args collects extra positional arguments.
**kwargs collects extra keyword arguments.
Parameters can be positional-only.
Parameters can be keyword-only.
def greet(name, message="Hello")
return f"{message}, {name}"
def total(*numbers)
return sum(numbers)
def configure(**options)
Avoid mutable objects as default parameter values when mutation would persist across calls.
SECTION 31: SCOPE
Local variables normally belong to the current function scope.
Global variables belong to module scope.
Python resolves names according to nested scopes.
The LEGB rule describes common name lookup order.
LEGB stands for Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.
The global keyword can assign to a module-level variable from inside a function.
The nonlocal keyword can assign to a variable in an enclosing function scope.
Prefer passing data into functions and returning results rather than relying heavily on global state.
SECTION 32: LAMBDA
A lambda expression creates a small anonymous function.
Lambda functions contain a single expression.
Lambdas are commonly used for short callbacks and sorting keys.
square = lambda x: x * x
sorted(names, key=lambda name: len(name))
Prefer normal def functions when logic becomes complicated.
SECTION 33: COMPREHENSIONS
List comprehensions create lists from iterable data.
Set comprehensions create sets.
Dictionary comprehensions create dictionaries.
Comprehensions can contain filtering conditions.
Comprehensions can transform each element.
[x * 2 for x in numbers]
[x for x in numbers if x > 0]
{x * x for x in numbers}
{name: len(name) for name in names}
A comprehension often replaces a simple loop used to construct a collection.
SECTION 34: BUILT-IN FUNCTIONS
len() returns a size or length.
print() writes output.
input() reads text input.
type() returns an object's type.
isinstance() checks type membership.
int() converts a value to an integer when possible.
float() converts a value to a float when possible.
str() converts a value to a string.
bool() converts a value to a Boolean.
list() creates a list from an iterable.
tuple() creates a tuple from an iterable.
set() creates a set from an iterable.
dict() creates a dictionary.
sum() adds numeric values.
min() returns a minimum value.
max() returns a maximum value.
abs() returns absolute value.
round() rounds a number.
sorted() returns sorted data.
reversed() returns a reverse iterator.
enumerate() adds indexes to iteration.
zip() combines iterables.
range() creates a range object.
any() tests whether any item is truthy.
all() tests whether every item is truthy.
map() applies a function to items.
filter() selects items according to a condition.
SECTION 35: ENUMERATE
enumerate() produces pairs containing an index and an item.
enumerate() is useful when both position and value are needed.
for index, value in enumerate(values)
print(index, value)
Prefer enumerate() over manually maintaining an index in many loops.
SECTION 36: ZIP
zip() combines elements from multiple iterables.
zip iteration normally stops when the shortest input is exhausted.
zip() is useful for processing related sequences together.
for name, score in zip(names, scores)
print(name, score)
SECTION 37: SORTING
sorted() returns a new sorted list.
list.sort() sorts a list in place.
Both sorted() and sort() accept a key function.
reverse=True sorts in descending order.
Python sorting is stable.
Sorting can be based on multiple criteria using tuple keys.
sorted(words, key=len)
sorted(numbers, reverse=True)
sorted() does not modify the original list.
sort() modifies the original list.
SECTION 38: EXCEPTIONS
An exception represents an error or unusual condition during execution.
Python can handle exceptions with try and except.
finally runs after exception handling whether or not an exception occurred.
else in exception handling runs when no exception occurs in the try block.
raise explicitly raises an exception.
Exception is the base class for many ordinary exceptions.
ValueError indicates an inappropriate value.
TypeError indicates an inappropriate type or operation between types.
IndexError indicates an invalid sequence index.
KeyError indicates a missing dictionary key.
FileNotFoundError indicates that a requested file was not found.
ZeroDivisionError occurs when dividing by zero.
NameError occurs when a name is not defined.
AttributeError occurs when an object lacks a requested attribute.
ImportError and ModuleNotFoundError can occur when imports fail.
number is int(user_input)
print("Invalid number")
Catch specific exceptions when possible.
Avoid using bare except unless there is a strong reason.
Do not silently ignore important exceptions.
SECTION 39: CUSTOM EXCEPTIONS
Custom exceptions can be created by subclassing Exception.
class InvalidScoreError(Exception)
Custom exceptions allow programs to communicate domain-specific errors.
Custom exceptions can be caught with except.
SECTION 40: FILE HANDLING
Python can read and write files.
open() opens a file.
File mode "r" means read.
File mode "w" means write and replaces existing contents.
File mode "a" means append.
File mode "x" attempts to create a new file.
Binary mode uses b.
Text encoding can be specified.
with is recommended when opening files because it closes the file automatically.
with open("notes.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file
text is file.read()
read() reads the entire file.
readline() reads one line.
readlines() reads lines into a list.
write() writes text.
writelines() writes multiple strings.
Prefer with open(...) as file for ordinary file handling.
Specify encoding="utf-8" when appropriate for text files.
SECTION 41: PATHLIB
pathlib provides object-oriented filesystem paths.
Path represents a filesystem path.
Path.exists() tests whether a path exists.
Path.is_file() tests whether a path is a file.
Path.is_dir() tests whether a path is a directory.
Path.mkdir() creates a directory.
Path.read_text() reads text.
Path.write_text() writes text.
Path.iterdir() iterates through directory contents.
Path.rglob() recursively searches for matching paths.
Path.glob() searches using patterns.
Path.name gives the final name.
Path.suffix gives a file extension.
Path.parent gives the parent path.
pathlib provides a modern interface for filesystem paths.
Path objects can be used with many standard library APIs.
SECTION 42: JSON
JSON is a common text format for structured data.
Python's json module can encode Python data into JSON.
json.load() reads JSON from a file.
json.loads() reads JSON from a string.
json.dump() writes JSON to a file.
json.dumps() converts Python data to a JSON string.
JSON commonly represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null.
Python dictionaries commonly correspond to JSON objects.
Python lists commonly correspond to JSON arrays.
Python None corresponds to JSON null.
Python True corresponds to JSON true.
Python False corresponds to JSON false.
data is {"name": "Alice", "score": 95}
SECTION 43: CSV
CSV stands for comma-separated values.
Python provides the csv module for reading and writing CSV data.
csv.reader() reads CSV rows.
csv.writer() writes CSV rows.
csv.DictReader() reads rows as dictionaries.
csv.DictWriter() writes dictionaries as rows.
CSV is useful for tabular data.
CSV is commonly used with spreadsheets and data analysis.
SECTION 44: MODULES
A module is a Python file containing definitions and executable statements.
import loads a module.
from module import name imports a specific name.
Modules help organize code.
Modules can contain functions.
Modules can contain classes.
Modules can contain constants.
Modules can contain executable initialization code.
from pathlib import Path

SECTION 46: CLASSES
A class defines a type and can describe data and behavior.
An object is an instance of a class.
Classes can contain attributes.
Classes can contain methods.
__init__ is commonly used to initialize an object.
self refers to the instance for ordinary instance methods.
Methods are functions defined inside classes.
Objects can have their own state.
def __init__(self, name)
A class is a blueprint or definition for instances.
An instance attribute belongs to a particular object.
A method usually operates on an object.
SECTION 47: OBJECT-ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects and classes.
Encapsulation groups data and behavior.
Inheritance allows one class to derive from another.
Polymorphism allows different objects to respond to a common operation.
Abstraction focuses on important interfaces while hiding unnecessary implementation details.

Composition is often preferable to deep inheritance hierarchies.

A class can inherit from another class.
The inherited class is commonly called the base class or parent class.
The inheriting class is commonly called the derived class or child class.
super() can access behavior from a parent class.
A child class can override inherited methods.
def speak(self)
class Dog(Animal)
Dog inherits from Animal.
Dog can override Animal.speak.
SECTION 49: PROPERTIES
The @property decorator can expose a method through attribute-like syntax.
Properties can control access to computed or validated data.
A property can have a getter.
A property can have a setter.
A property can have a deleter.
Properties can preserve a simple interface while controlling internal behavior.
SECTION 50: CLASS METHODS
@classmethod creates a method that receives the class as its first argument.
The conventional first parameter of a class method is cls.
Class methods can act as alternative constructors.
SECTION 51: STATIC METHODS
@staticmethod creates a method that does not automatically receive self or cls.
Static methods can group utility behavior inside a class when that organization is useful.
SECTION 52: DATACLASSES
The dataclasses module can reduce boilerplate for classes primarily storing data.
@dataclass can automatically generate methods such as __init__ and __repr__.
Dataclasses can contain type annotations.
Dataclasses can have default values.
Dataclasses can be frozen to discourage mutation.
SECTION 53: TYPE HINTS
Python supports optional type hints.
Type hints document expected types.
Type hints can improve editor support.
Type hints can help static type checkers.
Python normally does not enforce ordinary type hints at runtime.
list[int] can describe a list of integers.
dict[str, int] can describe a dictionary with string keys and integer values.
str | None can describe a value that may be a string or None in modern Python syntax.
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int
Type hints improve documentation.
Static type checking is different from runtime type enforcement.
SECTION 54: GENERICS
Generic type hints describe reusable type relationships.
TypeVar can represent a type variable.
Generic classes can work with multiple types while preserving type relationships.
Modern Python typing provides generic collection syntax.
SECTION 55: ITERABLES
An iterable is an object that can provide its values one at a time.
for loops operate on iterables.
Iterators implement the iterator protocol.
iter() obtains an iterator from an iterable when possible.
next() requests the next item from an iterator.
StopIteration signals the end of an iterator.
Every iterator is iterable.
Not every iterable is itself an iterator.
SECTION 56: GENERATORS
A generator produces values lazily.
Generator functions use yield.
yield pauses a generator and preserves its state.
Generators can save memory when processing large streams of data.
Generator expressions resemble list comprehensions but use parentheses.
def count_up_to(limit)
while number <= limit
A generator produces values on demand.
A generator avoids constructing all results at once.
SECTION 57: DECORATORS
A decorator modifies or wraps a function or class.
Decorators use the @ syntax.
Functions are first-class objects in Python.
A decorator commonly accepts a function and returns a wrapped function.
functools.wraps helps preserve metadata of wrapped functions.
Decorators are built on Python's support for higher-order functions.
SECTION 58: CLOSURES
A closure is a function that remembers values from an enclosing scope.
Nested functions can access variables from enclosing functions.
nonlocal can modify a variable in an enclosing function scope.
SECTION 59: FUNCTIONAL PROGRAMMING
Functions can be stored in variables.
Functions can be passed as arguments.
Functions can be returned from other functions.
map() transforms iterable values.
filter() selects iterable values.
functools.reduce() combines values into one result.
Lambda expressions can create short functions.
SECTION 60: RECURSION
Recursion occurs when a function calls itself.
A recursive function needs a base case.
The base case stops recursion.
Recursive calls should move toward the base case.
Excessive recursion can cause RecursionError.

Why use exceptions?
Exceptions allow errors and unusual conditions to be reported and handled separately from ordinary logic.
Why use type hints?
Type hints improve documentation, editor support, and compatibility with static analysis tools.
Why use tests?
Tests provide repeatable checks that program behavior matches expectations.
Why use logging?
Logging records runtime events and problems in a form useful for diagnosis and monitoring.
Why use virtual environments?
Virtual environments isolate project dependencies and reduce conflicts between projects.
SECTION 133: ADVANCED QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
What is a closure?
A closure is a function that retains access to variables from an enclosing scope.
What is a decorator?
A decorator is a callable mechanism that wraps or modifies another function or class.
What is a context manager?
A context manager controls setup and cleanup around a block of code.
What is polymorphism?
Polymorphism allows different objects to support a common operation or interface.
What is memoization?
Memoization caches results of previous function calls to avoid repeated computation.
What is dynamic programming?
Dynamic programming solves problems by reusing solutions to overlapping subproblems.
What is asynchronous programming?
Asynchronous programming allows a program to coordinate work that may pause while waiting for operations to complete.
What is multiprocessing?
Multiprocessing runs code in separate processes, each with its own memory space.
What is a race condition?
A race condition occurs when program behavior depends on the timing of concurrent operations accessing shared state.
What is refactoring?
Refactoring changes internal code structure while preserving intended external behavior.
